newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sumitomo sinks into the red over copper scandal.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo sinks into the red over copper scandal.

text.p: Sumitomo Corp posted the first loss in its history on Tuesday as huge copper losses pushed the otherwise healthy trading giant deep into the red.
But low domestic borrowing costs helped Japan's other big trading houses enjoy higher profits for the half-year period.

Sumitomo suffered a group net loss of 212.12 billion yen ($1.89 billion) -- the first loss since it was founded in 1919 -- after posting a special loss in the six months to September to tackle some of the damage left by the copper scandal.

The trading house fired its chief copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka in June and accused him of racking up losses, now estimated at $2.6 billion, on unauthorised trades. Sumitomo predicted it would also land in the red to the tune of 147 billion yen ($1.31 billion) in the full year as it continued to deal with the copper fallout.
"We took the Hamanaka scandal very seriously. We are striving to carry out bold in-house reforms," Takehiko Yonezu, an executive vice-president at the firm, told a news conference.
Sumitomo posted a special group loss of 289.1 billion yen ($2.58 billion) for the half-year period, including a special copper-related loss of 284.8 billion yen ($2.54 billion).

Of the big five trading firms , only Sumitomo reported group profits on Tuesday. The others -- Mitsubishi Corp, Mitsui & Co Ltd, Marubeni Corp and Itochu Corp -- enjoyed comfortable growth in parent profits thanks to greater income from financial deals as a result of low domestic interest rates.

But they all saw their half-year sales drop as they stopped reporting the entire value of precious metals trading in their sales accounts. Instead, they reported only the balance between the value of sales and purchases of precious metals.
Mitsubishi's parent current profit rose 22.5 percent to 35.72 billion yen ($318 million). Its net profit also rose.

"Although the domestic economic environment remained difficult and the outlook uncertain, our broad business base has provided stability and we remain on course to meet our initial projections for the full year," Tetsuo Kamimura, a Mitsubishi executive vice president, said in a statement.

Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities, while net profit is obtained by subtracting extraordinary profit or losses from current earnings and then deducting income tax.
Mitsubishi marked a total of 18.03 billion yen ($160 million) in extraordinary losses for the half-year period due partly to write-offs of problem loans to its affiliates.
It forecast a current profit of 70 billion yen ($625 million) for the full year, up 4.7 percent from a year ago.
A Mitsubishi spokesman said the company did not post any special loss for the half-year period related to troubled Nippon Leisure Card-System, owned 19 percent by Mitsubishi.

The maker of prepaid cards for "pachinko" pinball gaming machines lost 18 billion yen ($160 million) in the half-year period due to forgery of its pre-paid pinball cards. It lost 55 billion yen ($491 million) for the same reason in the full year which ended on March 31 this year, the spokesman said.

Mitsui, meanwhile, posted a 12 percent rise in its interim parent profit to 29.46 billion yen ($263 million) and predicted a 2.6 percent rise in the full-year profit to 62 billion yen ($553 million). Marubeni enjoyed a 27 percent surge in its interim profit, which rose to 20.48 billion yen ($182 million), and predicted a two percent rise in the full-year profit to 40 billion yen ($357 million). Itochu Corp's profits rose 11 percent to 20.17 billion yen ($180 million) and it forecast full-year profit would stay flat. ($1=112 yen)
